description: Single source of truth for the Starbird harm score rubric. Imported by src/lib/harmScore.ts (app) and scripts/verify-harm-score.py (Guardian). Changing this file is the only supported way to evolve the rubric. Update the bucket definitions, the inputs explanation, and the scope table together when ranges change. v2 (2026-09) added scope and role: scope bounds a score to the reach of the harm, role sets how much of an owner's score a brand inherits. See docs/harm-score-recalibration-2026-09.md.

inputs.label: Scope
inputs.detail: How far the harm reaches — the single strongest input. This is now a structured field on every firm (narrow / single_company / multi_company / systemic) and it hard-bounds the score: a single-contract vendor cannot exceed 65 no matter how ugly the contract, and a firm whose harm spans a portfolio cannot fall below 60. 73,000 Toys 'R' Us workers weighs more than one store closure.

inputs.label: Role
inputs.detail: Whose conduct the score describes. An `actor` causes the harm itself (Palantir, GEO Group, ExxonMobil). An `owner` causes it through portfolio companies — so a brand it owns is largely a victim, and inherits only part of the score. `both` operates and owns.

inputs.label: Permanence
inputs.detail: Recoverable vs irreversible. A pollution event that clears in a year is different from PFAS contamination. A brand-name reputation hit fades; a bankruptcy that closes every US store does not.

inputs.label: Intentionality
inputs.detail: Accidental vs strategic. Dividend recaps and sale-leasebacks are deliberate value extraction, not accidents.

inputs.label: Pattern
inputs.detail: One incident vs repeated behavior. A firm with multiple bankrupt portfolio companies scores higher than a firm with one.

inputs.label: Evidence
inputs.detail: Contemporaneous, sourced reporting beats unsourced claims. A score without a documented source is a weak score — and under v2 it can no longer buy a high one, because a thin record usually means a narrow scope.

buckets.label: Minimal
buckets.description: A small-scale concern with limited documentation, or a firm tracked here because it is *aligned* rather than harmful. The 0-19 band is where the aligned firms sit.
buckets.example: Patagonia (7), Costco (8) — the aligned end of the scale.

buckets.label: Moderate
buckets.description: Documented harm at a constrained scale. One bad incident, or a small pattern affecting hundreds rather than thousands. Rarely used — a narrow-scope vendor with real documentation usually lands in 55–65.
buckets.example: A mid-size firm with a handful of documented wage-theft complaints.

buckets.label: Significant
buckets.description: Thousands affected across multiple incidents, OR systematic behavior at a smaller scale. Most PE catch-alls and mid-tier firms land here.
buckets.example: JAB Holding (55) — quality degradation across Panera/Krispy Kreme/Peet's over ~a decade.

buckets.label: Severe
buckets.description: Tens of thousands affected, or a clear pattern of sale-leasebacks, mass layoffs, or environmental damage with sourced reporting.
buckets.example: Blackstone and BlackRock (70, systemic floor); Amazon (70); Aurelius (70) — The Body Shop bankruptcy.

buckets.label: Extreme
buckets.description: Documented mass layoffs (10,000+), portfolio-wide bankruptcies, or a well-established systematic pattern with multiple high-profile casualties.
buckets.example: Apollo Global (80), Ares (82), Cerberus (90), Advent (86), KKR (88) — Toys 'R' Us collapse, 73,000 jobs.

buckets.label: Catastrophic
buckets.description: Company-ending collapses or multiple simultaneous portfolio bankruptcies at the highest documented scale. Reserved for the worst-case outliers.
buckets.example: Leonard Green (97) — Joann (19,000+ layoffs 2025) + Container Store (Dec 2024) + Prospect Medical collapse, in the same window. Palantir (98) — state surveillance infrastructure at national scale.

scopes.label: Narrow
scopes.description: One contract, one site, one incident; a small vendor whose recorded harm is a single relationship.
scopes.example: Lemoine Disaster Recovery, LLC — one ICE-adjacent contract. Scored 83 before v2.

scopes.label: Single company
scopes.description: One company's own conduct. Substantial operator, but the harm does not extend past it.
scopes.example: Avelo Airlines — a scheduled carrier for which deportation charters are one line of business.

scopes.label: Multi-company
scopes.description: A portfolio, a conglomerate, or a multi-subsidiary operator. Most PE funds and large processors land here.
scopes.example: Purdue Pharma (93); Tyson Foods; every PE fund under $100B AUM.

scopes.label: Systemic
scopes.description: Economy-wide reach or historic scale. Reserved for entities whose harm is structural, not contained.
scopes.example: Palantir (98), Leonard Green (97), GEO Group (95), Blackstone and BlackRock (floored to 70).
